label: Conics and Perspectivity
notes: Open by stating the chapter's surprise: a quadratic curve turns out to behave like a one dimensional projective line. Preview the road map across printed pages 167 to 188 — Steiner generation, viewpoint independent cross ratio, the preserving group, Hesse transfer, and the Pascal and Brianchon pair. Stress that everything reduces to brackets.

label: Five Points Determine a Conic
notes: Remind students a conic carries six coefficients but only five up to scale, so five general points pin it down. Contrast the two constructions: the linear nullspace of the design matrix, and the bracket pencil joining two degenerate line pairs. Emphasize that the pencil view explains why four points leave a one parameter family.

label: Perspectivity versus Projectivity
notes: Draw the key distinction sharply. A perspectivity between two pencils fixes the cross axis and forces all meets onto one line. A projectivity is a composition of perspectivities and need not fix that axis. The whole chapter hinges on the non perspective case, where the meets escape a line and curve.

label: Steiner's Generation of a Conic
notes: State Steiner's theorem as the heart of the chapter: pair the lines of a pencil at A with the lines of a pencil at B by a projectivity, and the intersection points trace a conic through A and B. Walk the diagram, matching colored rays and showing the locus. Note a perspectivity would collapse this to a straight line.

label: The Generation Sweep
notes: Connect the theorem to the notebook's interactive sweep. A shared parameter on the circle induces the projective pairing between the two bundles, so each frame produces one meet with a near zero conic residual. Tell students the residual check is what certifies the locus is genuinely the conic and not an artifact.

label: Cross-Ratio From a Conic Point
notes: Introduce the cross ratio of four conic points measured by the four secants drawn from a fifth point on the curve. Write the bracket ratio explicitly. The theorem to feature: this value is independent of the vantage point, so the conic carries a well defined projective coordinate just like a line does.

label: Why the Value Is Invariant
notes: Explain the invariance as the engine of the chapter. Because the four secant angles change projectively as the viewpoint slides, their cross ratio stays fixed, and this is exactly the statement that the conic is a model of the real projective line. Mention the notebook's flat invariant tracker as numerical evidence.

label: Conics as Projective Lines
notes: Make the identification precise: parameterize the parabola by the Veronese map sending a parameter pair to its squares. A Mobius matrix on the parameter lifts to a three by three matrix preserving the conic form up to det squared. So conic preserving maps act like PGL of two on the curve. This is the group statement.

label: Hesse's Transfer Principle
notes: Present Hesse transfer as the bridge to incidence theorems. A line is recorded by its two meets with the conic, turning a line into a point pair. On the parabola the chord through parameters a and b crosses the axis at minus their product, so equal products encode concurrence as a quadrilateral set relation.

label: Pascal's Mystic Hexagon
notes: State Pascal: inscribe any hexagon in a conic, intersect the three pairs of opposite sides, and the three meets are collinear on the Pascal line. Trace the hexagon in the figure, color the three opposite side pairs, and mark the line. Stress this holds for any hexagon ordering, giving many Pascal lines.

label: Brianchon and Duality
notes: Give Brianchon as the exact point line dual of Pascal: circumscribe a hexagon of six tangents, and the three diagonals joining opposite vertices are concurrent. Emphasize the same join and meet bracket arithmetic tests both, so duality is not decorative — it halves the proof work and reuses one incidence equation.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Close by tying the threads: five points fix a conic, projective pencils generate it, its cross ratio is viewpoint free, its symmetries are PGL of two, and Hesse transfer reduces Pascal and Brianchon to one dimensional bracket identities. Send students to the notebook artifacts to replay each numerical certificate themselves.
